doc.title: Phoebe Jacobs and Jackie Harris interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 21, 2006

title: Range of New Orleans musicians: Kidd Jordan, Payton, Andrews
summary: Harris explains New Orleans musicians move among traditional, creative and electronic styles, naming Nicholas Payton, Branford, Donald Harrison, Troy Andrews and others.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: I think I was under a misconception about New Orleans and kind of what goes on there musically. And I don’t think I’m alone. And that is it occurred to me when I put on a recent CD by Kidd Jordan and the music he was playing was like something John Coltrane had not thought of. And so I realized that I didn’t really know what was coming out of that city.

Well let me start by saying the creative music community is clearly not as large as straight ahead or traditional jazz is. But New Orleans jazz covers every facet of jazz music which we have heard. And artists, young artists, as they develop for the most part, they really go through those different phases of jazz — playing jazz music until they reach the one that they are most comfortable with and the one that they decide that they want to make a career and play. But then too if you look at Nicholas Payton, so Nicholas’s father, Walter Payton, you could say he’s a traditional jazz artist but he’s also a blues artist or he’s also a rhythm & blues artist. So Nicholas plays trad, he plays contemporary, but then also he has done electronic. Then look at Branford, he’s done the same thing. Donald Harrison Jr. now has a smooth jazz CD which he gave me a couple of copies of it last week so he says to me look, I’m going to give you this, you probably don’t like it but I know this — I know you don’t like this but you know I’m doing this now too. I mean and Donald is the son of a Mardi Gras Indian chief, Donald Harrison Sr., and Donald plays Mardi Gras music as well. I mean Aaron Neville did a jazz CD a year before last with Irvin Mayfield. I mean you can see—
Look at Elvis Costello, what he’s doing with this.

Yeah. With Allen Toussaint. You know you just can’t, on any given day it’s kind of like football, on any given day you can’t imagine what or where you may see a New Orleanean playing. Troy “Trombone” Andrews’ roots are in traditional jazz music. I mean he was playing the trombone on the streets of New Orleans in brass bands when he was eight years old, maybe even five, the trumpet was taller than he was. He goes out with Lenny Kravitz now.
And how about Harry Connick Jr.? Look at how colorful his career’s been.
